Subscribe Close The Space Force is on the cusp of launching its next batch of satellites into low-Earth orbit as officials are laying the groundwork to connect future “enclaves” of platforms that are expected to pass critical data to warfighters. The Space Development Agency over the past year has been building out a so-called Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture ( PWSA ) that will consist of multiple layers of data transport and missile tracking satellites manufactured by multiple vendors. SDA is planning to add to it next week with the launch of 21 Northrop Grumman-made birds. “We launched our first plane last September with York [Space Systems]. We launched a second with Lockheed [Martin] in October. Then we took a strategic pause … and then we launched the second plane of York back in July. So with that, we have three planes on orbit, 63 satellites, and [with] our next one now we bring in a third vendor on the transport side” with Northrop’s systems, Gurpartap “GP” Sandhoo, director of SDA and the Space Force’s portfolio acquisition executive for missile warning and tracking, told reporters during a call ahead of next week’s launch. Liftoff is scheduled for Oct. 5 at 1:15 a.m. Pacific Time from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. Advertisement “This will be the fourth launch, and we have six more to go. We have two more in transport, then we have four in tracking. The goal here is to build out this mesh on the data transport side, and then once we start launching our sensors in a tracking layer, this is what they’ll connect to to deliver that missile warning, tracking and defense data to the warfighter,” Sandhoo explained. The upcoming launch is about adding capacity to what’s already on orbit. “To get to a global coverage we have to have the capacity. To get to a resilient, survivable architecture we have to have enough capacity up there,” Sandhoo said, noting that “the whole point” of the PWSA is to boost the survivability of the U.S. military’s satellite posture to address concerns that adversaries could target American platforms on orbit during a future conflict. “We’ll have additional capacity. We’ll have persistent regional coverage at the end of Tranche 1. At the end of Tranche 2, we’ll have persistent global coverage. So, it’s absolutely a capacity issue. The capability is already up there, but it’s not up there as fully intended and designed,” he told DefenseScoop during the call with reporters. Meanwhile, the Pentagon has been planning for a so-called Space Data Network featuring military-owned and commercial satellites manufactured by different companies that would enable a multi-orbit communications architecture. Advertisement In May, the department awarded SpaceX a $2.3 billion contract to deliver an operational prototype for the SDN’s “backbone” by the end of next year. Other transition agreements have also been awarded to Lockheed, Northrop, Rocket Lab and Amazon LEO for Government to demonstrate ground-to-space and space-to-space data transport between platforms that were built by disparate vendors. Sandhoo told reporters that the PWSA and SDN will provide the military with different “enclaves” of systems. “The initial SDN satellites are the SpaceX satellites, right?” he said. “We will be doing some technical risk reduction [to address issues related to] how do we actually connect to talk to them. We are starting on that process, working with the [space-based sensing and targeting portfolio acquisition executive].” “With Tranche 1 and Tranche 2 [of the PWSA] we’ll have an enclave,” he continued. “The SpaceX [contribution to the Space Data Network] is going to be one enclave. We’ll have another enclave. At some point we need to start connecting these enclaves to make sure that data can flow between the multiple enclaves. And there may be other commercial entities that come on into the market in 2, 3, or 4 years from now, and it’ll be smart for us to make sure that we can connect to all of them to make sure … this information can flow as much as possible. So yeah, we are in active risk-reduction activities to make sure we can connect with them.” Share Facebook LinkedIn Twitter Copy Link Add to Preferred Sources Advertisement Advertisement More Like This Advertisement Top Stories Advertisement More Scoops (Image credit: Northrop Grumman) (Getty Images) SpaceX Falcon 9 launches the Space Development Agency T1TL-C mission to low-Earth orbit from Space Launch Complex 4E at Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif., Oct. 15., 2025. Beginning in 2027, T1 will provide initial warfighting capability to deliver regional persistence for tactical military data channels, along with advanced missile tracking and missile warning, and beyond-line-of-sight targeting plus demonstration of UHF and S-band tactical satellite communications. live_web_research.page_text: Forterra partners with Hypercraft on autonomous vehicle for high-risk missions MilTech Forterra partners with Hypercraft on autonomous vehicle for high-risk missions By Riley Ceder Wednesday, Oct 14, 2026 The Hypercraft Razorback autonomous ground vehicle comes equipped with Forterra's AutoDrive autonomous software platform. (Courtesy of Forterra) Defense companies Forterra and Hypercraft have collaborated to produce a contested-environment-ready autonomous vehicle, which they showed off for the first time at the Association of the U.S. Army Annual Meeting and Exposition in Washington, D.C. Forterra installed its AutoDrive autonomy software platform that powers unmanned maneuverability onto Hypercraft’s Razorback ground vehicle, yielding a product that can withstand the punishing logistics of combat without putting soldiers at risk. “The point of an autonomous military vehicle is to deliver payloads to the point of friction,” Forterra Chief Growth Officer Scott Sanders said. “Razorback has the power, power generation and capacity to carry a wide variety of weapons systems without modification.” Forterra’s AutoDrive autonomous driving system has become an industry standard, integrated on more than 200 vehicles in active service. Meanwhile, the Razorback weaponizes 300 horsepower, 4,0000 volumes of payload range, a 500-mile range and up to 38 kilowatts of distributable power. Forterra was the first U.S. ground autonomy company to be actively deployed in Ukraine and has completed 88 casualty evacuation missions to rescue Ukrainian soldiers from the front lines, according to Forterra spokesperson Kelsey Szablowski. That mission to not put military personnel in harm’s way is part of Forterra’s mantra. “Robots don’t bleed,” Szablowski said. The Army has taken notice of the company’s approach. In August, the service selected Forterra as a prime contractor for its Engineer Autonomous Breaching Capability program, a larger effort to field autonomous vehicles during mine-clearing missions. The company outfitted a Ford F-250 with its AutoDrive technology and named it the Mobile Autonomous Uncrewed Lanemaker, or MAUL. The MAUL, which hosts no human in the driver’s seat and can drive autonomously or be controlled by an operator, is made for reconnaissance, planning and clearing in mine-contested environments. The autonomous vehicle deploys a rocket-propelled mine-clearing line charge, or MICLIC, to detonate explosives in an area before driving through. In mid-August, Forterra demonstrated the MAUL’s capabilities during Project Sandhills at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, in which drones attacked the vehicle as it attempted to mine-detect and clear. The MAUL fought off and destroyed the drones with an onboard automated turret, while it navigated through the area autonomously. The exercise took place from Aug. 17 to Aug. 28 and demonstrated the Army’s ability to tackle a myriad of mission sets using attributable autonomous systems that reduce risks to soldiers. “Instead of relying solely on high-value, crewed assets, we can field semi-autonomous F-250s, sUAS swarms and autonomous c-UAS systems that are adaptable, scalable and resilient,” said Capt. Denny Drummey, Sandhills Project operations officer, during the exercise. live_web_research.page_text: DIU and DAWG Launch Autonomous Vehicle Orchestrator Prize Challenge Skip to main content January 13, 2026 (Washington, D.C.) - Autonomous systems are maturing into distributed, multi-domain forces across the Department of War. As this arsenal grows, so does the need for an operationally viable Autonomous Vehicle Orchestrator – a layer of technology that can translate a battlefield commander’s intent from voice, text, and haptic input into machine execution. To support this critical DoW need, the Defense Innovation Unit, the Defense Autonomous Warfare Group (DAWG), and the United States Navy are launching a $100,000,000 prize challenge to prototype market-ready solutions to establish a robust, scalable and vehicle-agnostic capability for understanding, tasking and coordinating autonomous systems at the fleet level. “The Department’s fleet of autonomous vehicles is the future of warfighting - but they are nothing without the intelligence and experience of the operator. This Prize Challenge will deliver a human-machine interaction layer that will directly impact the lethality and effectiveness of these systems,” said Hon. Michael Dodd, Acting Deputy Director of DIU and Assistant Secretary of War for Critical Technologies. The challenge will include iterative sprints, tackling increasingly complex portions of the problem. “We want orchestrator technologies that allow humans to work the way they already command – through plain language that expresses desired effects, constraints, timing, and priorities – not by clicking through menus or programming behaviors,” said LtGen Frank Donovan, Director of the DAWG. “We must ensure the human - the ethical decision maker - always maintains a clear understanding of what the system is doing and why. As we continue down this path, we want to integrate effects at increased speed and tempo, at a time and place of our choosing, to overwhelm our adversaries.” Vendors will only be eligible for selection prior to the first sprint, and, upon successful completion of the previous sprint, can progress to the next sprint. Vendors who are not able to complete the sprint will not move forward. “This solicitation’s approach is the new standard—we’re moving fast to deliver tangible capabilities to the warfighter. Selected performers will be shoulder‑to‑shoulder with operators, and they will be proving that their capability works in an operational environment,” said Hon. Emil Michael, Acting Director of DIU and Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering. “If a company can deliver, they will receive substantial rewards. If they can’t, we will move on. The ones who show they can perform will move immediately into follow‑on contracts so we can field these capabilities at scale for our fighting force.” Up to $100,000,000 in awards are available for this effort and the government anticipates multiple awards. The Challenge will be open through January 25th, 2026.

selected_records.title: Space Force laying groundwork to connect future satellite ‘enclaves’ as it prepares for additional launches

article.body:
Space Force satellite mesh advances; no autonomous-vehicle deployment reported

The Space Development Agency’s Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture is a satellite network, not an autonomous-vehicle programme. Three planes, carrying 63 satellites, were on orbit, with a launch of 21 Northrop Grumman satellites scheduled for Oct. 5, according to the report. The planned network is intended to connect data-transport satellites with future missile-tracking platforms. Officials said Tranche 1 is intended to provide persistent regional coverage, with persistent global coverage planned for Tranche 2. The story provides no vehicle, autonomy stack, road operating domain, vehicle safety record, or autonomous-transport service status.
